questions.q: According to DAMA's Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK), what is data quality?
options: The degree to which data is fit for its intended purpose(s)
The percentage of fields in a table that are not NULL
The absence of any typos or formatting errors
The total number of rows that have been validated
questions.explain: DMBOK defines quality as fitness for use â€” relative to a specific purpose, not an absolute standard of perfection.

questions.q: A customer's billing system lists them in "NY" and the shipping system lists the same customer in "New York." Both values are individually valid. Which dimension is failing?
options: Consistency â€” the same fact disagrees with itself across systems
Validity â€” neither value conforms to a format rule
Completeness â€” a value is missing
Uniqueness â€” the customer appears twice
questions.explain: Consistency asks whether the same real-world fact, stored in more than one place, says the same thing everywhere â€” here it doesn't, even though both individual values are valid.

questions.q: What are the five stages of the data quality lifecycle, in order, per this lesson?
options: Profile, define, measure, remediate, monitor
Define, profile, remediate, measure, monitor
Measure, remediate, profile, define, monitor
Monitor, profile, define, measure, remediate
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs: profile (discover what's there) â†’ define (turn findings into rules) â†’ measure (run the rules) â†’ remediate (fix problems) â†’ monitor (watch continuously).

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key difference between 'profiling' and 'defining' a data quality rule?
options: Profiling describes what the data actually contains without judgment; defining decides whether that's acceptable
Profiling and defining are two names for the exact same activity
Defining always happens before profiling in the lifecycle
Profiling is only used for financial data, defining for all other data
questions.explain: Profiling is discovery (e.g. 'this column is 3% NULL'); defining is the judgment call, made in the define stage, about whether that rate is acceptable.

questions.q: If COUNT(*) returns 10,000 but COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) returns 9,850 on a table where CustomerID should be unique, what does this most likely indicate?
options: There are likely duplicate CustomerID values â€” a uniqueness problem
The table has exactly 150 NULL rows
The query has a syntax error
CustomerID is not a valid column name
questions.explain: When total row count exceeds the distinct count of a column meant to be unique, that gap typically signals duplicate values â€” the uniqueness dimension from Lesson 2/15.

questions.q: If MAX(LEN(EmailAddress)) exactly equals a VARCHAR column's declared maximum length, what should that make you suspect?
options: That some values may have been truncated at insert time
That the column definitely has zero NULL values
That every email address in the table is identical
That the column is missing from INFORMATION_SCHEMA entirely
questions.explain: Values packed right up against a column's declared maximum length are a strong hint that longer values are getting cut off when inserted.

questions.q: What does a LEFT JOIN from a child table to its parent table, filtered to WHERE <parent key> IS NULL, find?
options: Orphaned rows â€” child rows whose foreign key value has no matching row in the parent table
Every row that has a NULL value in the child table's primary key
Duplicate rows in the parent table
Rows where the parent and child tables have identical column names
questions.explain: This is the standard T-SQL pattern for finding orphaned rows â€” child rows pointing at a foreign key value that doesn't exist in the parent table.

questions.q: What does "accuracy" measure as a data quality dimension?
options: How closely a value reflects the real-world fact it represents
Whether a value matches an expected format or data type
Whether a value is missing or present
Whether a value is duplicated elsewhere in the table
questions.explain: Accuracy is about truth â€” whether the stored value matches reality â€” not about format or presence, which are other dimensions (validity and completeness).

questions.q: Why does checking only `WHERE Email IS NULL` risk undercounting missing data?
options: It misses empty strings and sentinel values like 'N/A' that also represent missing data
IS NULL is not valid T-SQL syntax
It only works on the first row of a table
NULL values are always converted to zero automatically in SQL Server
questions.explain: An empty string is not NULL, so IS NULL misses it. Sentinel values like 'N/A' or '1900-01-01' look like real data to a plain count but represent the same missingness.

questions.q: What does validity measure?
options: Whether a value conforms to a defined rule â€” type, format, range, or allowed set
Whether a value matches the real-world fact it represents
Whether a value is missing from a required column
Whether a value agrees with the same fact stored elsewhere
questions.explain: Validity asks whether a value is a 'legal' value according to a rule, not whether it's true (accuracy), present (completeness), or consistent with another copy (consistency).

questions.q: In `GROUP BY Email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, what does the `HAVING` clause do that a `WHERE` clause couldn't in this query?
options: It filters on an aggregated value (COUNT) computed after grouping, which WHERE cannot do
It removes NULL values from the Email column before grouping
It sorts the results by Email alphabetically
It converts the Email column to uppercase for comparison
questions.explain: HAVING filters groups based on an aggregate result like COUNT(*); WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation and cannot reference an aggregate like COUNT(*) directly.

questions.q: What are the four parts of a well-documented data quality rule, per this lesson?
options: Scope, condition, severity, and owner
Table, column, index, and primary key
Accuracy, completeness, consistency, and validity
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and GROUP BY
questions.explain: Scope defines what's covered, condition defines pass/fail, severity defines urgency, and owner defines who's responsible for acting on failures.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing the WHERE clause for the failure condition rather than the success condition?
options: A check's purpose is to find rows that need attention, not to confirm rows that are already fine
SQL Server only allows WHERE clauses that evaluate to false for good rows
Writing a success condition is always slower to execute
It's required syntax for UNION ALL queries
questions.explain: A check query is meant to surface problems. Selecting the bad rows directly (rather than the good ones) is both the more useful output and the habit the lesson recommends building.

questions.q: Which SQL pattern does the lesson use to find orphaned child rows?
options: LEFT JOIN the child to the parent, then filter for rows where the parent's key is NULL
INNER JOIN the child to the parent, then filter for rows where the parent's key is NULL
A subquery using EXISTS that always returns TRUE
GROUP BY the parent key with HAVING COUNT(*) = 0
questions.explain: A LEFT JOIN keeps all child rows even when no matching parent exists; filtering for a NULL parent key after the join identifies exactly the orphaned rows â€” an INNER JOIN would simply drop them instead of surfacing them.

questions.q: What is the difference between a hard threshold and a tolerance band?
options: A hard threshold is a single line that triggers failure when crossed; a tolerance band is a range, with failure triggered in either direction outside it
A hard threshold can only be used with COUNT(); a tolerance band can only be used with SUM()
A tolerance band always has a wider acceptable range than a hard threshold
They are the same concept with different names
questions.explain: A hard threshold has one direction of failure (e.g. more than 50 missing addresses). A tolerance band has two (e.g. order count outside 950-1050) â€” both too high and too low are suspicious.

questions.q: What does the 5 Whys technique actually involve?
options: Repeatedly asking "why" until you reach a fundamental, actionable cause, usually around five times
Writing exactly five SQL queries to find a problem
Interviewing five different stakeholders
Running a rule five times to confirm it's broken
questions.explain: 5 Whys is a simple iterative questioning technique, not a fixed number of queries or interviews.

questions.q: How does monitoring differ from the one-time rule checks taught in Chapter 4?
options: Monitoring runs the check on a schedule, stores a history, compares results to an expected range, and alerts automatically instead of requiring someone to run it by hand
Monitoring uses a completely different query language than rule checks
Monitoring only applies to pipeline jobs, never to data values
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: A rule check answers whether data is bad right now; monitoring answers that continuously, without anyone needing to ask.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a scorecard and a dashboard, as described in this lesson?
options: A scorecard answers 'are we on track' at a glance for executives; a dashboard provides the detailed breakdowns and drill-through an analyst needs to investigate
A dashboard only works with manual data; a scorecard only works with automated data
They are identical, just different names for the same thing
A scorecard always shows more detail than a dashboard
questions.explain: A healthy program typically needs both: a scorecard for quick status and a dashboard underneath it for investigation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a data quality issue needs to be formally tracked rather than just mentioned informally?
options: An untracked issue has no owner, no priority, no due date, and no way to confirm months later that it was actually fixed
Formal tracking is only required by certain government regulations
Informal mentions are always more accurate than tracked records
Tracking is only needed for issues with zero business impact
questions.explain: Issue management turns a one-time mention into something trackable and closeable.

questions.q: Which three data quality dimensions, together, were involved in the Northfield Outfitters problem?
options: Uniqueness, consistency, and completeness
Timeliness, validity, and accuracy
Only uniqueness, with no other dimensions involved
Security, privacy, and availability
questions.explain: Uniqueness (duplicate rows), consistency (name formatting), and completeness (missing emails from POS) all appeared together.
